tasks.q: What is the purpose of a language translator?
a: Process source code into a form or operations that can be executed
Guarantee that every algorithm is correct
Draw the user interface automatically
Replace the processor
tasks.fb: A translator enables execution. Correct outputs still need to be tested.

tasks.q: A program translates but calculates the wrong discount. What is still needed?
a: Testing and correction of its logic
A claim that translation guarantees correctness
Deletion of the requirements
A faster monitor
tasks.fb: A valid expression can perform the wrong calculation.

tasks.q: Put a successful compiled workflow in order.
steps: Compile the source for a target platform
tasks.fb: If a build fails, correct the reported problem and compile again before running the updated result.

tasks.q: A developer changes a calculation in the source. What updates the compiled release?
a: Recompile and distribute the new build
Run the old executable and expect its instructions to change
Rename the source file only
Remove the editor
tasks.fb: The existing compiled file does not update itself when its source changes.

tasks.q: In this model, what happens when interpretation reaches an invalid instruction?
a: It reports the error and stops at that point
It silently fixes the instruction
It proves earlier output was correct
It always generates a distributable executable
tasks.fb: Earlier valid instructions may already have run. Real implementations can also perform checks before execution.

tasks.q: Why can repeated interpretation have an execution cost?
a: Source processing happens during each run
The screen must redraw the entire source
Interpreters cannot use memory
All source is converted to an image
tasks.fb: Compiled code can avoid repeating the same translation work at runtime. Actual performance depends on the implementation.

tasks.q: Investigate both modes with the error, repair it, then successfully run both modes.
The interpreter displayed 6 before stopping. What can you conclude?
a: At least one earlier output instruction executed
The entire program completed successfully
The compiler must also have displayed 6
There are no logic errors
tasks.fb: Partial output is evidence of earlier execution, not evidence that the entire program works.

tasks.q: Match each need to the approach it most directly supports.
items: Create a saved target-code build before users run it
Process source instructions during each run
Distribute the translated program without supplying high-level source
Use the simplified statement-at-a-time edit-run cycle
tasks.fb: Both can be used during development; the choice depends on the language tools and project requirements.

tasks.q: Which claim about compiled releases needs correcting?
a: They work on every processor and operating system without checking
They may need rebuilding after source changes
They can be distributed as target code
They can avoid repeated source translation on each run
tasks.fb: Compiled output usually targets a particular platform and may depend on runtime support.

opts: A compiler can produce a saved target-code build
An interpreter processes source during execution
Every interpreted program is slower than every compiled program
correct: A compiler can produce a saved target-code build
An interpreter processes source during execution
tasks.fb: Avoid universal speed claims; use the stated translation models when comparing the approaches.

tasks.q: What should a developer do after fixing an error?
a: Rerun relevant tests using the corrected program
Assume the change cannot affect anything else
Keep distributing only the failed build
Remove all error messages
tasks.fb: Testing the correction checks both the intended fix and other affected behaviour.

tasks.q: A team distributes a stable application to a known platform. Which benefit supports compilation?
a: Users can run the translated build without compiling its source
It guarantees no logic errors
The source changes automatically update all installed copies
The executable runs on every instruction set
tasks.fb: Compilation can support distribution, but does not remove testing or platform requirements.

tasks.q: Match each statement to the approach.
pairs: Translates the source before running its compiled result
Processes source while carrying out its instructions
tasks.fb: These are the GCSE comparison models. Some real implementations combine compilation and interpretation.

info.title: Why translate
info.text: The processor executes machine instructions, not the high-level source as written. A translator connects source instructions to operations the computer can carry out. Translation does not prove that the program meets its requirements. Think: Why is translating a program different from testing it?

info.title: Compile before running
info.text: In the GCSE model, a compiler translates the whole source program before execution. A successful build produces target code that can be saved and run again. Changes to the source require a new build to update that compiled version. Think: Why can a user run a compiled release without the original compiler?

info.title: Interpret during execution
info.text: In the simplified GCSE model, an interpreter processes and executes source statement by statement. If an error is reached, execution stops there and reports the problem. The interpreting software is used again when the source is run again. Think: Why can an interpreter be useful while a programmer is making frequent changes?

info.title: Observe the error
info.text: Use the same small program in both modes. The simulator deliberately models whole-program compilation and statement-at-a-time interpretation. Some real systems combine techniques; this is a conceptual comparison, not a timing benchmark. Think: Record what each mode outputs before the deliberately invalid instruction is fixed.

info.title: Development and distribution
info.text: Interpretation can support a quick edit-run-debug cycle. A compiled release can be distributed without giving users the high-level source. Target compatibility and runtime dependencies still matter for a compiled program. Think: Give one reason a supplier might compile a stable release for a specified platform.

info.title: Compare without absolutes
info.text: Both approaches can help identify errors, but neither guarantees correct logic. A compiler may report several translation errors from a build. An interpreter can help locate a problem during execution; error behaviour depends on the tool and error type. Think: Why is “a compiler finds every mistake” an unreliable claim?
